title: Domain learning at a human experience budget

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a learner that acquires genuinely new domain-specific structure from an apprenticeship-scale quantity of relevant experience. Examples include learning a constructed language, operating an unfamiliar laboratory instrument, or reasoning within a formal system with newly specified axioms. The central capability is efficient acquisition when the target domain’s particular rules have been withheld from prior training. This is a synthesis of the proposed concept.

Reusable general learning priors can contribute to this capability. An evaluation would therefore need an operational definition of which target-specific regularities were withheld and which prior knowledge the learner could use. A human-scale budget also needs a domain-specific definition covering the evidence available to the learner, its opportunities for interaction, and repeated exposure. BabyLM supplies a concrete language-learning precedent through restricted corpus sizes and, in its 2026 challenge, cumulative-exposure limits.

In-context learning and abstraction-benchmark performance can involve transfer, recombination, and new inference. Their scores alone leave unresolved how much relevant prior evidence enabled the result. Establishing this innovation requires controlled evidence about acquisition under a restricted experience budget. ARC’s interactive adaptation tasks and BabyLM’s limited-data training tasks examine relevant aspects, while the supplied evidence leaves the full proposed cross-domain demonstration unestablished.

significance.text: Conditional significance assessment. A general method for learning previously withheld domain structure from an apprenticeship-scale stream would substantially expand machine learning in settings with limited evidence. In domains where the capability is demonstrated, competence with less domain-specific data follows directly. Lower acquisition costs would also become possible when collecting or labeling that evidence is a substantial expense.

Conditional downstream possibilities include rare-disease research, individually configured robots, new scientific apparatus, bounded workplace tasks, and private environments where large public datasets are unavailable. Each application would still depend on access to sufficiently informative observations, appropriate interfaces, and validation suited to its consequences. Medical reliability, autonomous operation, and discovery of empirical laws would require additional demonstrations beyond successful domain acquisition.

The human-apprenticeship analogy supplies a motivating scale for experience. Its interpretation depends on the modality, feedback, prior knowledge, and opportunities for active exploration available to each learner. BabyLM’s childhood-language estimate motivates a language budget near 100 million words. It supplies no established conversion between words, physical interaction hours, or examples, and its limited-data benchmark successes show that meaningful progress already occurs within constrained corpora.

Acquisition efficiency, parameter efficiency, computational cost, and power consumption are separate dimensions of impact. The 2026 BabyLM findings explicitly distinguish the first three resource considerations. A learner could use little new domain evidence while consuming substantial training or inference compute, so any claimed resource benefit would need its own measurements. The supplied evidence also leaves open how broadly an advance demonstrated in several domains would transfer to other settings.

missing_breakthrough.text: The target capability is reliable acquisition of withheld domain-specific regularities from a small, explicitly accounted stream of relevant experience. The supplied studies motivate this research goal and document progress in language learning and adaptation benchmarks. They leave unresolved whether an existing method already satisfies the complete cross-domain proposal. Continuing research activity alone cannot establish field-wide noncompletion.

Scientific synthesis. A central barrier is selecting useful representations and hypotheses from sparse evidence while retaining enough flexibility to learn unfamiliar rules. The learner must infer which observations reveal stable structure, determine which distinctions matter for future tasks, and apply what it learns to combinations absent from its experience. In interactive domains, selecting informative actions becomes part of the learning problem.

Scientific synthesis. Limited evidence also creates an identifiability boundary. Several candidate rules may explain the same observations and produce different predictions elsewhere. Successful acquisition therefore depends on informative experience, suitable general priors, or access to discriminating interventions. Sample efficiency cannot guarantee competence when the permitted evidence leaves the relevant alternatives unresolved.

Evaluation-design synthesis. Establishing the advance requires separating useful general priors from prior access to the target rules. Contamination can enter through pretraining, later training, demonstrations, retrieval systems, auxiliary models, or evaluation feedback. A credible experiment needs a traceable account of these routes and a precise description of what knowledge each system could access.

Engineering barriers include accounting for distinct evidence, repeated processing, feedback, and computation without treating corpus size as a complete measure of experience. BabyLM’s 2026 cumulative-exposure limits address repeated passes explicitly. Extending that discipline across language, physical interaction, and formal reasoning would require separately specified budgets and human comparisons appropriate to each domain.

current_state.text: The December 2023 Findings of the BabyLM Challenge describes a substantial language-learning data-efficiency gap and reports that contemporary language models typically used three or four orders of magnitude more data than children. Its Section 2 attributes an estimate of fewer than 100 million word tokens encountered by age 13 to Gilkerson et al. 2017. That developmental paper was absent from the supplied evidence, so the estimate is available here through BabyLM’s attribution. Sections 3–4 define the Strict track at 100 million words and Strict-Small at 10 million words.

The 2023 challenge permitted repeated exposure to those corpora and reported strong small-data benchmark learning. Its Strict-track discussion describes a leading submission outperforming the Llama 2 and RoBERTa-Base comparison systems on the relevant evaluation suite. The scope of that result is the tested language benchmarks. The supplied paper extraction ends on page 29 of 34, with the cited budget definitions and performance discussion available in the retained material.

The fourth BabyLM findings, dated October 29, 2026, continues to frame the challenge around closing the human–machine language-learning data-efficiency gap. It retains corpus ceilings of 100 million words for Strict and 10 million for Strict-Small. It additionally limits cumulative exposure, counting repeated passes, to 1 billion words for Strict and 100 million for Strict-Small. Hidden tasks supplement the public evaluation suite to assess generalization. The supplied review had a complete extraction of this paper.

The Llama 3 technical report, available as an arXiv report with the supplied version revised November 23, 2024, states that its flagship model had 405 billion trainable parameters and was pretrained on 15.6 trillion text tokens using 3.8 × 10^25 FLOPs. It attributes performance gains principally to data quality, diversity, and increased training scale. These figures characterize that model family. The supplied extraction truncates in Section 5.1.3, while the cited training statements are complete.

Dividing Llama 3’s 15.6 trillion training tokens by a reference budget of 100 million words yields 156,000 tokens per reference word. This calculated scale comparison mixes tokenizer tokens with words and does not measure equivalent learning evidence. Differences in modality, repetition, data quality, and prior learning also affect interpretation of a human–machine experience comparison.

The saved ARC Prize results page lists GPT-6, dated September 2, 2026, at 95.0% on ARC-AGI-2 and 99.95% on ARC-AGI-3. The detailed leaderboard identifies GPT-6 Astra and distinguishes ARC-AGI-3 Standard performance of 62.7% from Provider Adapter performance displayed as 99.9%. Its explanation describes an adapter that preserves reasoning state and compacts conversations. The near-ceiling result is consequently dependent on the evaluation harness. The differing displayed precision leaves the two adapter figures compatible in the supplied review.

ARC-AGI-3 evaluates adaptation to novel interactive environments, and the leaderboard emphasizes efficient problem solving with limited resources. The supplied ARC pages leave GPT-6’s pretraining corpus size unspecified and provide no demonstration that the reported scores were acquired using only an apprenticeship-scale quantity of relevant evidence. The evaluations were not independently rerun. The review used the retained leaderboard text, with its plotted visualization uninspected.

Evidence-scope synthesis. These dated observations establish continued limited-data research, particular small-data benchmark achievements, a documented large-scale training example, and harness-dependent adaptation scores. The supplied freshness search record is empty. Consequently, this record cannot establish a comprehensive frontier assessment or field-wide noncompletion as of November 1, 2026. The proposed innovation remains a capability target whose full completion is unestablished by these inputs.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration. Evaluators construct at least three held-out domains, such as a constructed language, a physical apparatus with unfamiliar dynamics, and a formal system with new axioms. They preregister the tasks, success measures, and withholding procedures. Documentation should show how target-specific rules and evidence were withheld from every training stage and auxiliary system, while identifying the reusable general priors available to the learner.
completion_criteria.label: At least three preregistered domains with target-specific rules withheld

completion_criteria.text: Proposed experience limits. For a language domain, an upper limit of 10^8 words is motivated by BabyLM’s childhood-language estimate and corpus-budget design. Evaluators would separately specify a budget of a few hundred interaction hours for interactive domains. The interaction-hour threshold is a proposal, and the two limits have no established equivalence. Each protocol should report distinct evidence, total exposure including repetitions, and all permitted demonstrations and feedback.
completion_criteria.label: Experience capped at 10^8 words or a few hundred interaction-hours

completion_criteria.text: Proposed feedback and comparison rules. The experiment would prohibit a per-task reward written by the experimenters and specify permissible feedback in advance. Human apprentices would receive comparable relevant exposure, with differences in prior knowledge, modality, and interaction opportunities documented. Success would mean reaching a preregistered human-apprentice performance threshold on the domain’s held-out tests. The proposal uses apprenticeship-scale experience and sets no one-to-ten-example mastery requirement.
completion_criteria.label: Preregistered human-apprentice performance reached without experimenter-written per-task rewards

completion_criteria.text: Proposed generalization tests. Evaluation should include held-out recombinations of learned rules, with hidden tasks protecting against adaptation to the public test suite. BabyLM’s 2026 hidden evaluations provide a precedent for testing beyond public benchmarks. The particular three-domain requirement and human-apprentice success threshold are proposed choices whose adequacy would need justification for the intended claim.
completion_criteria.label: Learned rules generalize to held-out recombinations on hidden tasks

completion_criteria.text: Proposed controls and reproducibility. Report a frozen frontier-model baseline and a from-scratch baseline alongside the learner, with their evidence access and evaluation conditions explicit. Record auxiliary-model contributions, training compute, test-time compute, repeated exposure, and the complete interaction history. Independent evaluators should reproduce the result using additional withheld domain instances and repeated runs, with enough protocol and artifact access to audit contamination and budget compliance.
completion_criteria.label: Independent reproduction across additional withheld instances with auditable resource accounting

completion_criteria.text: Proposed interpretation boundary. Passing would establish demonstrated acquisition breadth across the tested domains and conditions. Claims about broader applicability would require additional evidence. Results should identify failure cases, dependence on informative feedback, and practical data and compute costs. Deployment-specific reliability, intervention robustness, and power efficiency would each require corresponding demonstrations.
completion_criteria.label: Reported applicability limits reflect tested conditions and documented failures

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis. MLC-01, A predictive theory of what deep networks learn, could explain which representations and priors support efficient acquisition and predict when a restricted evidence budget will suffice. MLC-02 concerns the demonstrated learning capability. A predictive theory and a successful acquisition method have separate completion requirements.

Roster-based synthesis. MLC-03, Cumulative learning without forgetting or loss of plasticity, concerns retaining competence and the ability to learn across a sequence of experiences. It could enable repeated apprenticeship-scale learning over a system’s lifetime. MLC-02 focuses on the evidence required to acquire a domain, leaving long-run retention and plasticity as additional questions.

Roster-based synthesis. MLC-04, World models that survive novel interventions, overlaps when an acquired domain model must support unfamiliar actions or causal changes. MLC-02’s acquisition tests can include held-out recombinations. Establishing reliable predictions under novel interventions would require tests designed for MLC-04’s causal robustness objective.

Roster-based synthesis. MLC-05, Local credit assignment that matches backpropagation at scale, concerns the mechanism for assigning learning credit. Such a mechanism might contribute to efficient acquisition. MLC-02 permits any learning mechanism that satisfies its evidence-controlled demonstration, while MLC-05 requires evidence about local learning and performance at scale.

Roster-based synthesis. MLC-06, Algorithmic legibility sufficient to verify and edit a model, could help inspect acquired rules and audit the influence of prior knowledge. Its objective is understanding and modifying model computation. MLC-02’s behavioral acquisition evidence would leave that degree of internal legibility unresolved.

Roster-based synthesis. MLC-07, Open-ended curricula that create externally verified new competencies, concerns generating a continuing sequence of productive learning challenges. An efficient domain learner could use those curricula, while a curriculum could expose the learner to informative experience. MLC-02 bounds the evidence used for specified domains, and MLC-07 asks whether curriculum generation sustains verified competency growth.

Roster-based synthesis. MLC-08, Discovery of new empirical laws, confirmed by experiment, could benefit from efficient learning with unfamiliar scientific apparatus or limited observations. Its completion requires a new empirical law and experimental confirmation. Acquiring competence in a scientific domain would establish only part of the capabilities needed for that outcome.

Roster-based synthesis. MLC-09, Skill learning from scarce, irreversible, real-world outcomes, shares the problem of limited informative experience. It adds the practical constraint that some outcomes carry irreversible consequences and cannot be freely repeated. MLC-02’s proposed constructed and controlled domains allow acquisition efficiency to be studied under a wider range of interaction conditions.

Roster-based synthesis. MLC-10, Non-vacuous behavioral certificates at frontier scale, concerns credible guarantees about behavior within specified conditions. MLC-02 would supply finite empirical evidence of acquisition and generalization. A behavioral certificate would require its own formal or verification basis and an explicit scope of validity.

Roster-based synthesis. MLC-11, Frontier competence at a biological-order power budget, concerns the energy required to sustain competence. MLC-02 concerns the amount of relevant experience required to acquire it. Both could contribute to a more resource-efficient learner, with separate measurements needed for experience, computation, and power. These relationships are inferred from the supplied roster titles and the reviewed MLC-02 material.

change_log.change: Preserved MLC-02’s identity and expanded its definition around acquisition of withheld domain-specific regularities with reusable general priors explicitly allowed.
change_log.reason: This retains the proposed innovation while making the boundary between target-specific knowledge and general learning ability operational.

change_log.change: Revised the exclusive account of in-context learning and benchmark success to allow transfer, recombination, and new inference.
change_log.reason: The supplied evidence does not isolate their contributions or establish that all such performance consists of prior-knowledge reuse.

change_log.change: Qualified the claim that the complete capability remains missing across the field.
change_log.reason: The supplied freshness search record is empty, and continuing research does not establish comprehensive noncompletion.

change_log.change: Integrated the 2023 BabyLM small-data achievements, repeated-exposure allowance, and the 2026 cumulative-exposure limits.
change_log.reason: These details distinguish corpus size from total exposure and preserve evidence of meaningful existing progress.

change_log.change: Retained the childhood-language estimate through BabyLM’s attribution and disclosed the absent developmental source and partial 2023 extraction.
change_log.reason: The supplied review verifies BabyLM’s statement while leaving its developmental basis independently unchecked.

change_log.change: Preserved Llama 3’s parameter, token, and compute figures and expressed the calculated comparison as 156,000 tokens per reference word.
change_log.reason: The arithmetic is supported, while incompatible units prevent interpreting it as an equivalent-evidence learning ratio.

change_log.change: Reconciled the ARC results-page scores with the detailed Standard and Provider Adapter results.
change_log.reason: The near-ceiling ARC-AGI-3 score depends on the harness, and the pages leave GPT-6’s pretraining scale unspecified.

change_log.change: Removed universal claims about frontier models requiring large corpora and additional test-time search, and qualified downstream applications.
change_log.reason: The sources document particular systems and results. Medical, robotic, and scientific applications require further informative evidence, interfaces, and validation.

change_log.change: Expanded the proposed demonstration with contamination controls, domain-specific budgets, human comparisons, feedback rules, compute accounting, and reproducibility requirements.
change_log.reason: These details make the evaluation auditable and preserve the distinction between proposed thresholds and established standards.

change_log.change: Added explicit limits on what finite multi-domain tests establish and mapped relationships to every other supplied roster entry.
change_log.reason: Demonstrated breadth supports bounded conclusions, and the related concepts retain distinct objectives. Full records for the other concepts were unavailable.

unresolved_issues: The supplied evidence does not establish whether any existing system satisfies the full proposed capability as of November 1, 2026.
An operational definition of withheld domain-specific structure is still needed, including treatment of general priors and indirect exposure through auxiliary systems.
The proposed few-hundred-hour interaction budget lacks supplied empirical calibration. Its relationship to a human apprenticeship and to the language budget remains open.
Comparable human exposure requires a protocol addressing prior knowledge, embodiment, feedback, and opportunities for active exploration.
The developmental basis of BabyLM’s under-100-million-word estimate remains independently unchecked because the cited Gilkerson paper was absent.
The permitted feedback under the proposed experimenter-written reward restriction requires precise specification.
The supplied ARC pages do not resolve GPT-6’s training evidence budget. The reported evaluations were not independently rerun, and the leaderboard visualization was uninspected.
Relationships to other roster entries are provisional because only their titles and the reviewed MLC-02 cross-references were supplied.

brief.title: Machines that learn new skills with an apprentice’s practice
possible: You could introduce a machine to an unfamiliar laboratory instrument and have it learn the operating rules through an apprentice’s amount of practice. The same capability would let it learn an invented language or reason with new mathematical rules that were kept out of its earlier training.
why: Researchers and workplaces could teach machines useful skills where examples are scarce or private. Collecting and labeling teaching material could cost less, making it easier to adapt machines to new scientific equipment, individually configured robots and bounded workplace tasks.

sources.who: Alex Warstadt, Aaron Mueller and collaborators
sources.showed: BabyLM participants trained language models on limited text. The strongest submissions beat comparison models trained on much larger collections on the language tests used.
sources.quote:
The winning submissions
using the LTG-BERT architecture (Samuel
et al., 2023) outperformed models trained on
trillions of words.
sources.cited_for: Language models can learn substantially from restricted amounts of text.
sources.not_established: Success on these language tests does not establish learning unfamiliar rules across different kinds of tasks.

sources.showed: BabyLM extended limited-text learning to multiple languages. It also capped repeated exposure to training text and added hidden tests of performance beyond public evaluations.
sources.quote:
This year’s winning submissions
to the new multilingual track also show that
LLM-generated parallel data can be effective at
improving multilingual capabilities in low-data
settings.
sources.cited_for: Repeated exposure can be counted, and hidden tests can probe learning beyond familiar evaluations.
sources.not_established: These results do not establish acquisition of previously withheld rules across language, physical interaction and formal reasoning.

sources.showed: Meta trained its flagship Llama model on 15.6 trillion tokens, the pieces of text models process. Its smaller models improved when trained longer than the amount judged best for their training computation.
sources.quote: The resulting models perform better than compute-optimal models at the same inference budget.
sources.cited_for: Large-scale training provides a reference for the goal of learning with much less relevant experience.
sources.not_established: Large-scale performance does not establish acquisition of unfamiliar rules within an apprentice’s experience budget.

sources.showed: ARC Prize reports near-perfect performance by OpenAI’s Astra model on its interactive adaptation test.
sources.cited_for: Machines achieve high scores on tests involving adaptation to unfamiliar environments.
sources.not_established: The score does not establish how much relevant evidence the model encountered during earlier training.

sources.showed: ARC Prize separates standard results from results using extra software around the model. Astra’s near-perfect result used software that preserves reasoning state and compacts conversations.
sources.cited_for: Performance on interactive adaptation tests depends partly on the software surrounding the model.
sources.not_established: The results do not establish learning within a fully counted apprenticeship-scale experience budget.

shown: BabyLM teams have demonstrated substantial language learning from limited text, with leading submissions outperforming much larger-data comparison models on the tested tasks. ARC Prize reports strong adaptation to unfamiliar interactive environments, with Astra’s near-perfect result depending on extra software around the model.
missing: A controlled demonstration across different kinds of tasks, with the unfamiliar rules excluded from all earlier training and helper systems, remains unestablished.
Learning within fully counted experience limits still needs comparison with human apprentices given comparable relevant exposure.
Independent teams still need to reproduce the full result on fresh tasks, with complete accounts of experience and computation.

milestones.label: Unfamiliar rules stay hidden across at least three domains
milestones.explanation: At least three areas of learning would have to have tasks, success measures and procedures for keeping rules hidden set in advance. This separates learning new rules from using earlier exposure.

milestones.label: Learning stays within the proposed experience limits
milestones.explanation: Language learning would have to stay within 100 million words, with a separate interaction-time cap and all repetitions, demonstrations and feedback counted. This makes the experience limit meaningful.

milestones.label: Performance reaches the agreed human apprentice threshold
milestones.explanation: The learner would have to reach a human apprentice threshold set in advance, with comparable exposure and no experimenter-written reward for each task. This tests competence under the proposed teaching conditions.

milestones.label: Learned rules work in unseen combinations
milestones.explanation: Hidden tests would have to show that the learner applies rules in combinations absent from its experience. This tests whether it learned reusable structure beyond familiar examples.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce results with complete resource accounts
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to repeat success on fresh instances against a fixed leading model and a model trained from scratch, accounting for all resources. This tests reproducibility and compliance with the limits.

milestones.label: Claims match tested conditions and documented failures
milestones.explanation: Results would have to identify failures, feedback needs and practical data and computation costs within tested conditions. This defines where the capability works and which broader claims need further demonstrations.

uncertain: The boundary between reusable general knowledge and prior exposure to the supposedly unfamiliar rules still needs a precise definition.
The proposed interaction-time cap has no established equivalence to the language budget or to a human apprenticeship.
Sparse observations may fit several conflicting rules; success depends on whether feedback and exploration can distinguish them.

page.title: Human-level sample efficiency
page.definition: A learning procedure acquires unfamiliar domain rules, reaching human reference performance from no more domain-specific experience than comparison humans. The target rules are withheld from earlier training, retrieval and auxiliary systems.

goal.need: A 2020 survey placed languages spoken by 1.2 billion people in its lowest category for digital language resources. In 2023, typical large language models used 1,000 to 10,000 times as much language data as children need. Where little text exists, learning from fewer examples could give students access to more books in their own language. It could also reduce the work of adapting speech recognition to a new microphone. Translation quality still depends on whether the available texts cover the vocabulary and usage readers need.

figures.caption: BabyLM 2026 text-only training limits
figures.note: Cumulative exposure includes repeated passes and text generated during training. These are competition budgets, not measured human-equivalence thresholds.

statements.quote: The BabyLM Challenge is a shared task aimed at closing the data-efficiency gap between human and machine language learners.

statements.body: DARPA, Learning with Less Labels programme
statements.quote: reduce the amount of data needed to adapt a model from millions to hundreds of labeled examples
statements.context: The programme target counts labeled adaptation examples.

statements.quote: We define AGI as a system’s ability to acquire any skill a human can, as efficiently as a human can.
statements.context: AGI means artificial general intelligence; this is the Foundation’s definition.

completion.title: One learner matches human performance and experience budgets on withheld language and interactive tasks.
completion.criterion: Under a published human-comparison protocol, the same learning procedure reaches at least the human reference performance on both unfamiliar language tasks and unfamiliar interactive rule-learning tasks. In each comparison it uses no more target-domain experience than the human participants. Count demonstrations, feedback and repeated exposure. Specify allowed general prior knowledge and exclude the target rules from earlier training, retrieval and auxiliary models.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas fallback; no common externally published completion test was located.
completion.basis: BabyLM limits pretraining data, and ARC-AGI-3 measures actions in unfamiliar games. The Foundation reports a semi-private ARC-AGI-3 score of 100.0% for GPT-6.2 Astra with the Provider Adapter. A separate experiment compares people and a model on an unfamiliar instruction grammar. Neither result measures the same learner’s performance and target-specific exposure in both domains.

milestones.title: A learner matches human accuracy after one example of an unfamiliar handwritten character.
milestones.criterion: Given one image of an unfamiliar character, select another instance of it from 20 distinct characters written by one person in the same alphabet. Across the 10 evaluation alphabets, the average error rate must be at most 4.5%. Use separate alphabets for background training.
milestones.set_by: Lake, Salakhutdinov and Tenenbaum, published Omniglot human-comparison protocol and Figure 6A; the reference concerns handwritten-character classification.

milestones.title: A model matches the 0.71 BabyLM reference score on at most 100 million pretraining words.
milestones.criterion: Under the 2023 BabyLM Strict rules, use only the supplied English corpus for pretraining and reach an aggregate score of at least 0.71, the published Llama 2 reference. BLiMP and its supplement together carry 50% of the score, with equal weight per subtask. (Super)GLUE carries 30% and MSGS 20%. The word limit applies to corpus size. Repeated passes are allowed, and downstream fine-tuning uses separate task data.
milestones.set_by: BabyLM Challenge organizers, 2023 Findings, section 5.4 and table 2. The threshold denotes parity with the higher published comparator. The competition ranks submissions by aggregate score.

milestones.title: An agent reaches a median human-normalized Atari score of 1 within 100,000 steps per game.
milestones.criterion: Train on each of the 26 Atari 100k games with at most 100,000 environment steps per game, or 400,000 frames at frame skip 4. For each game, subtract the random-agent reference from the agent’s score and divide by the human reference minus the random-agent reference. The median of the 26 normalized scores must be at least 1. Replay of collected experience and simulation inside a learned model are permitted.
milestones.set_by: Atari 100k benchmark community; budget and human-normalization convention documented by Ye and colleagues in Sections 5.1–5.2 and Table 1.

milestones.title: An agent scores 100% on ARC-AGI-3’s semi-private interactive environments.
milestones.criterion: Attain 100% Relative Human Action Efficiency on the ARC-AGI-3 semi-private set, specified as 55 environments. For each completed level, square the ratio of the upper-median first-time human action count to the agent’s action count and cap the score at 1.15. Weight levels by their number, starting at 1. Cap each game’s score at the fraction of total level weight completed, then average game scores equally. Only actions affecting the environment count.
milestones.set_by: ARC Prize Foundation, ARC-AGI-3 Scoring Methodology; 100% is its published human-efficiency reference.
milestones.threshold_quote: AI completes all games/levels while matching or surpassing human efficiency

milestones.title: A learner reaches 80.7% exact accuracy on new instructions from 14 examples in an artificial language.
milestones.criterion: Use Lake and Baroni’s 14 study instructions and 10 query instructions, with word and colour assignments randomized. Each answer is a sequence of coloured symbols. Count it as correct only if the whole sequence follows the test grammar. Match or exceed 80.7% exact accuracy across responses. Reserve the test grammar from training and validation, including versions equivalent under renaming input and output symbols. The 14 examples count distinct study pairs, including those people could revisit.
milestones.set_by: Brenden M. Lake and Marco Baroni, few-shot instruction-learning protocol and measured human reference, 2023.
milestones.threshold_quote: exactly matched the algebraic standard in 80.7% of cases

not_found: No common externally published completion standard combining cross-domain learning, withheld rules and fully counted human-comparable experience was located.
No published conversion between language words, environment actions and apprenticeship hours was located.
No recognized milestone ladder joining the language and interactive benchmark protocols was located.
The opened Astra reports do not supply its total target-relevant training experience or the semi-private environment count underlying the headline score.
No published result was found comparing one learner with people on both withheld language and interactive rules while counting all target-specific exposure.

results.finding: ELC-BERT scored 0.74 aggregate in 2023 BabyLM Strict with a 98.04-million-word pretraining corpus.
results.detail: The challenge organizers published the official track result in the CoNLL proceedings. ELC-BERT trained for over 450 epochs, and the Strict rules counted corpus size rather than repeated passes.

results.finding: BabySteps ranked first in the 2026 BabyLM Strict track under a 100-million-word corpus cap.
results.detail: The 2026 track also allowed multimodal data and interactive training, and capped cumulative exposure at 1 billion words, including repeated passes. The corpus cap is a track limit. The winner’s exact corpus size is unspecified.
results.quote:
Strict Track Winner.Satheesh et al. (2026) also
achieved the highest score on the Strict track.

results.finding: OpenAI’s GPT-6 scored 99.95% on ARC-AGI-3 (environment count unstated).
results.detail: The leaderboard links Astra, Sol, and Luna from a single GPT-6 row and gives one score for that row.

results.finding: GPT-6 Astra scored 99.9% on ARC-AGI-3 with the Provider Adapter harness. The environment count is unreported.
results.detail: The Provider Adapter harness preserves reasoning state and compacts longer conversations so the model can reuse prior work.

results.finding: Image-based AttentiveMatcher averaged 2.35% error on 20-way one-shot Omniglot across 10 test alphabets and 15 training seeds.
results.detail: Table 1 gives the numeric result. Section 4.1 identifies the predefined Omniglot episodes and uses the other ten Evaluation alphabets for validation.

results.finding: ELC-BERT scored 0.743 on BabyLM Strict using 98.04 million pretraining words.
results.detail: The source is a conference proceedings paper, classified under journal because the format has no proceedings category. The score comes from the official shared-task leaderboard.

results.finding: Full Context ConvARC reached 1.5% error on Omniglot with one example per character and 20 choices per trial.

results.finding: Bayesian program learning averaged 3.3% error across 10 alphabets on one-shot, 20-way handwritten-character matching.
results.detail: Background training used images and pen strokes. Evaluation used only raw images of novel characters.
results.quote:
BPL showed a similar
error rate of 3.3%, achieving better performance
than a deep convolutional network (convnet; 13.5%
errors) and the HD model (34.8%)

results.finding: MLC averaged 92.9% exact-match accuracy across 10 runs on Lake and Baroni’s 14-study-pair, 10-query instruction task.
results.detail: The separate novel-rule experiment excludes equivalent individual rules from meta-training and uses newly generated test episodes. It leaves the full grammar holdout for the 14-study-pair task unverified.
results.quote:
achieving a mean of 92.9% (SD = 8.2) exact match accuracy on the key few-shot
instruction task

goal.need = "A 2020 survey placed languages spoken by 1.2 billion people in its lowest category for digital language resources. In 2023, typical large language models used 1,000 to 10,000 times as much language data as children need. Where little text exists, learning from fewer examples could give students access to more books in their own language. It could also reduce the work of adapting speech recognition to a new microphone. Translation quality still depends on whether the available texts cover the vocabulary and usage readers need.". Reason: The current paragraph gives competition limits without identifying who lacks training data or what learning from fewer examples would make possible.

edit completion: criterion = "Under a published human-comparison protocol, the same learning procedure reaches at least the human reference performance on both unfamiliar language tasks and unfamiliar interactive rule-learning tasks. In each comparison it uses no more target-domain experience than the human participants. Count demonstrations, feedback and repeated exposure. Specify allowed general prior knowledge and exclude the target rules from earlier training, retrieval and auxiliary models."; basis = "BabyLM limits pretraining data, and ARC-AGI-3 measures actions in unfamiliar games. The Foundation reports a semi-private ARC-AGI-3 score of 100.0% for GPT-6.2 Astra with the Provider Adapter. A separate experiment compares people and a model on an unfamiliar instruction grammar. Neither result measures the same learner\u2019s performance and target-specific exposure in both domains."; refs = [1, 2, 4, 5, 17, 18]. Reason: The current test mixes its criterion with a verdict and omits the scope of the subsequently reported 100.0% interactive score.

edit m1: criterion = "Given one image of an unfamiliar character, select another instance of it from 20 distinct characters written by one person in the same alphabet. Across the 10 evaluation alphabets, the average error rate must be at most 4.5%. Use separate alphabets for background training."; threshold_quote = "error rate of 4.5% (N = 40)."; threshold_ref = 6. Reason: The existing quotation omits the numerical human reference, and the criterion includes the model’s result.

edit m2: title = "A model matches the 0.71 BabyLM reference score on at most 100 million pretraining words."; criterion = "Under the 2023 BabyLM Strict rules, use only the supplied English corpus for pretraining and reach an aggregate score of at least 0.71, the published Llama 2 reference. BLiMP and its supplement together carry 50% of the score, with equal weight per subtask. (Super)GLUE carries 30% and MSGS 20%. The word limit applies to corpus size. Repeated passes are allowed, and downstream fine-tuning uses separate task data."; set_by = "BabyLM Challenge organizers, 2023 Findings, section 5.4 and table 2. The threshold denotes parity with the higher published comparator. The competition ranks submissions by aggregate score."; threshold_quote = "Llama 2 0.84 0.84 0.26 0.75 0.71"; threshold_ref = 1. Reason: The original title excludes the 100-million-word boundary and turns a published comparison score into a requirement to beat it.

add milestone after m2: "A learner reaches 80.7% exact accuracy on new instructions from 14 examples in an artificial language.". Reason: The language milestones lack a test of whether a learner can infer withheld rules from examples and apply them to new instructions as accurately as people.

edit m3: criterion = "Train on each of the 26 Atari 100k games with at most 100,000 environment steps per game, or 400,000 frames at frame skip 4. For each game, subtract the random-agent reference from the agent\u2019s score and divide by the human reference minus the random-agent reference. The median of the 26 normalized scores must be at least 1. Replay of collected experience and simulation inside a learned model are permitted."; threshold_quote = "Normed Median 0.000 1.000"; threshold_ref = 7. Reason: The Atari criterion includes one agent’s score and seed count, while its quotation establishes only the interaction budget.

edit m4: criterion = "Attain 100% Relative Human Action Efficiency on the ARC-AGI-3 semi-private set, specified as 55 environments. For each completed level, square the ratio of the upper-median first-time human action count to the agent\u2019s action count and cap the score at 1.15. Weight levels by their number, starting at 1. Cap each game\u2019s score at the fraction of total level weight completed, then average game scores equally. Only actions affecting the environment count."; threshold_quote = "AI completes all games/levels while matching or surpassing human efficiency"; threshold_ref = 5; refs = [5, 19, 4, 17]. Reason: The current criterion embeds a September result and leaves out how the human reference, level weights and game caps determine a full score.
